paragraphs.text: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

Gathering with family allows our past and present selves to meet: There’s the familiar seat at the dinner table, the decades-old sibling rivalry, a parent’s instinct to remind their now-adult child to bring a jacket. Whether you’re returning to the home you grew up in or welcoming your own children back, reuniting can remind us of how much we’ve changed—and how easily we can slip back into the roles we once occupied.

In a 2024 essay, my colleague Faith Hill explored the complicated pull of our childhood home. In his research on the subject, the psychologist Jerry M. Burger found that even people who didn’t have a particularly happy childhood felt compelled to revisit the places they grew up. The desire to return, Faith explains, isn’t necessarily about reliving the good old days; it can also stem from a desire to reconnect with a version of ourselves that has become less familiar.

The holidays offer a rare opportunity to spend time with those who have known us through different stages of our life. Today’s newsletter explores what we might learn from revisiting the people we used to be.
Your Childhood Home Might Never Stop Haunting You
Many of us feel pulled toward the places where we grew up. But it can be weird when old and new selves collide. (From 2024)
When young people start their own life, they often miss where they came from. (From 2018)
Nostalgia Is a Shield Against Unhappiness
Happy memories have a uniquely protective power against a sad present. (From 2023)

• The timeless bliss of eating hometown food: For many holiday travelers, a trip back to where they grew up is a chance to revisit the local spots they spend the rest of the year craving, Hayley Glatter wrote in 2018.
• The new age of endless parenting: More grown kids are in near-constant contact with their family. Some call this a failure to launch—but there’s another way to look at it, Faith wrote in 2024.

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “I’ve always felt most in awe of the natural world out on the trail, in forests and on big mountain hikes. Then we got our first dog. At ten months old, he’s taught me to slow down, and our slow loops around the yard have shown me what I was walking past: a dahlia opening a little more each morning, a persimmon slowly turning orange. The wonder I used to travel for was here the whole time,” Julie L. writes.
We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.
